To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the motivation for drug seeking in the drug experienced user is influenced by the duration and intensity (dose) of pre-exposure, and the time elapsed since withdrawal from the drug.
repeated exposure to stimulants and opioids increases the motivation to obtain these drugs, and that the magnitude of this effect depends on the duration and intensity (dose) of pre-exposure.

repeated exposure to drugs of abuse induces neuroadaptations that increase the motivational value of cues previously paired with the drug, and that this increase in motivational value is dependent on the duration and intensity (dose) of pre-exposure and the time since the last exposure to the drug.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the factors that control the motivation to take drug of abuse in the experienced user.

the mechanisms that underlie the motivation to take a drug of abuse, and how this motivation is influenced by prior exposure to the drug, by the time since withdrawal from the drug, and by the presence of cues associated with drug exposure.
understanding how repeated pre-exposure to drugs can lead to changes in the brain that increase motivation to seek drugs and that can lead to relapse.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the motivation underlying relapse after long term abstinence is a complex phenomenon that is influenced by the interaction of a number of factors, including the duration and intensity and the type of drug used, the time since withdrawal, and the type of stressor used.

the reinitiation or relapse to drug taking after abstinence is the result of the complex interplay between drug-induced changes in the circuit of the brain that control the motivation to obtain the drugs, and changes that occur as a consequence of the repeated experience of the drug.

the motivation to take drug is increased after pre-exposure to drugs and that this effect is mediated in part by the effects of drugs on the brain systems that control appetitive and aversively motivated behavior.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
repeated pre-exposure to drugs of abuse can lead to a state of heightened motivation to take the drug that can persist for long periods of withdrawal.

the motivation to take a drug is determined by the interaction of a number of factors including: (1) the intensity and duration of drug use, (2) the time since withdrawal, (3) the nature of the drug, and (4) the context in which the drug is taken.
pre-exposure and abstinence from drugs of abuse can alter the brain's motivational systems in ways that make relapse to drug taking more likely.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of pre-exposure on the reinitiating drug seeking are likely to be the consequence of the induction of changes in both the appetitive and aversion motivational systems.
the motivation to obtain drugs is increased in individuals who have a history of drug use.

pre-exposure of rats to drugs such as cocaine, amphetamine, or morphine can induce changes in the brain circuitry that mediate appetitive and aversion motivational processes, and that these changes can persist for extended periods of time, even when the drug is unavailable.
